Psychology in film, literature and music

Ulysses and the sirens: tying yourself to the mast

Ulysses knew he would not resist the song, so he asked to be tied up. Psychology calls it precommitment.

In the Odyssey, Ulysses wants to hear the song of the sirens, which lures sailors onto the rocks. He knows that when he hears it, he will not be able to resist. So he plugs his crew's ears with wax and asks them to tie him to the mast and not release him even if he orders them to.

Deciding before temptation

Psychology and economics call this precommitment. We know our preferences change in the moment: in the morning we want to save, but in the afternoon we see a bargain. Committing in advance protects the planning self from the impulsive self. The philosopher Jon Elster devoted a book to the idea, Ulysses and the Sirens (1979).

Everyday examples are not keeping sweets at home, setting up automatic transfers to savings or leaving your phone in another room while studying. In mental health there are advance directives, sometimes called "Ulysses contracts": people write down their treatment preferences in case of a future crisis.

References

  1. Elster, J. (1979). Ulysses and the Sirens. Cambridge University Press.
  2. Ariely, D. y Wertenbroch, K. (2002). Procrastination, deadlines, and performance. Psychological Science, 13(3), 219–224.
